summary: A great power of the South Asian subcontinent with the world's largest population, birthplace of the Indus Valley civilization and of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism; it became independent from Britain in 1947 and is the world's largest democracy.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: The roots of Hinduism go back to the Vedic religion from about 1500 BC, which later developed into the Upanishads, the epics the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, and the Bhakti movement that spread widely in the Middle Ages, deeply woven into India's caste system, festivals and daily life. Although it went through Islamic dynasties and British colonial rule, the majority of the population has always remained Hindu. After the Partition of India and Pakistan in 1947, the Muslim-majority areas were assigned to Pakistan, making the Hindu proportion in India even higher, but the 1950 constitution still defined India as a secular state.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: In the 7th century Arab merchants were already active on the coast of Kerala in the south, and in 711 Arab forces conquered Sindh; the Delhi Sultanate was established in 1206, and from 1526 the Mughal Empire ruled northern India for more than three hundred years. Sufi saints attracted large numbers of people to convert in places such as Bengal and Punjab. At Partition in 1947 millions of Muslims moved to Pakistan, but more than thirty million remained in India, and today India's Muslim population exceeds two hundred million, concentrated in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Kerala and Jammu and Kashmir.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Tradition says the Apostle Thomas came to Kerala in the 1st century, and the local community of "Saint Thomas Christians" has a long history. The Portuguese occupied Goa in 1510, and in 1542 Saint Francis Xavier came to India to preach; in the British colonial period Protestant missions entered in large numbers. In the 19th century American Baptists and Welsh Presbyterians preached in the northeastern hills, making Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya Christian-majority states.

ranking.name: Sikhism
ranking.description: Sikhism was founded in Punjab by Guru Nanak (1469–1539), who advocated belief in one God and opposed the caste system. In 1699 the tenth guru, Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa order, in the early 19th century Ranjit Singh built the Sikh Empire, and in 1849 it was annexed by the British. At Partition in 1947 Punjab was split in two, and the Sikhs of West Punjab almost all moved into India; today Sikhs are concentrated in the state of Punjab.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhism was founded in India in the 5th century BC by Shakyamuni and was vigorously promoted by Ashoka in the 3rd century BC, but declined after the Middle Ages because of the Hindu revival and the destruction of monasteries such as Nalanda at the end of the 12th century. In 1956 Ambedkar, the drafter of the constitution, led hundreds of thousands of "Untouchables" in a mass conversion to Buddhism in Nagpur to escape caste oppression; in 1959 the Dalai Lama went into exile in India, which also brought large numbers of Tibetan Buddhists. Buddhists are found mainly in Maharashtra, Ladakh and Sikkim.

ranking.name: Jainism
ranking.description: Jainism arose in the same period as Buddhism and was propagated by Mahavira (Vardhamana) in the 6th–5th centuries BC, stressing extreme nonviolence (ahimsa). Because its doctrine forbids farming, which may harm living beings, Jains are mostly engaged in commerce and finance, and are concentrated in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra; though few in number, their economic influence is great, and Gandhi's thought of nonviolence was also influenced by them.

religion.background: India is the birthplace of four major religions: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism. The religion of the Vedic age evolved into Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism arose in the 6th–5th centuries BC, Buddhism flourished in the time of Ashoka, and the later Hindu revival caused Buddhism to decline in its homeland. From the 7th century Islam came through trade and conquest, and the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire ruled northern India for hundreds of years; in the 15th century Sikhism was born in Punjab; Portuguese and British colonization brought Christianity. The Partition of India and Pakistan along religious lines in 1947 caused mass migration and violence, and independent India has made secularism the founding principle of the state, but the relationship between religion and politics remains an important issue to this day.

language.official: The official languages of the Union are Hindi and English, and the constitution also recognizes 22 scheduled languages.

ranking.name: Hindi
ranking.description: Hindi derives from the dialects around Delhi and in the Mughal period fused with Persian and Arabic into "Hindustani". During British rule in the 19th century, Hindi, written in Devanagari and favoring Sanskrit vocabulary, gradually parted ways with Urdu, written in the Persian script. The 1950 constitution made Hindi the official language of the Union, with English used alongside it; in 1965 protests against the forcible imposition of Hindi broke out in the southern state of Tamil Nadu, which allowed the status of English to be retained. Statistically its speakers also include northern Indian dialects such as Bhojpuri, and Hindi films (Bollywood) have made it a language understood across the country.

ranking.name: Bengali
ranking.description: Bengali is spoken mainly in West Bengal and in Tripura in the northeast. In the 19th century the "Bengal Renaissance" arose in Calcutta, the capital of British India, and in 1913 Tagore became the first Asian Nobel laureate in literature, for his Bengali poetry. At Partition in 1947 Bengal was split in two, and the eastern part became today's Bangladesh.

ranking.name: Marathi
ranking.description: Marathi is the language of Maharashtra in the west, and the Maratha Empire founded by Shivaji in the 17th century used it as its administrative language. After independence Bombay State included the two language regions of Marathi and Gujarati; after the "Samyukta Maharashtra movement" it was divided into two states in 1960, with Bombay assigned to Maharashtra.

ranking.name: Telugu
ranking.description: Telugu belongs to the Dravidian family and is spoken in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. In 1952 the activist Potti Sreeramulu died fasting to demand a Telugu-speaking state, leading to the establishment of Andhra State in 1953, the first Indian state formed on a linguistic basis, and prompting the nationwide redrawing of state boundaries by language in 1956.

ranking.name: Tamil
ranking.description: Tamil is one of the oldest languages still in use in the world; "Sangam literature" can be traced back about two thousand years, and in 2004 it became the first language in India to be officially recognized as a "classical language". Tamil Nadu has a strong tradition of Dravidian nationalism, and movements against the compulsory imposition of Hindi broke out in the 1930s and again in 1965.

ranking.name: Gujarati
ranking.description: Gujarati is the language of Gujarat in the west and was also the mother tongue of Mahatma Gandhi. Gujarati merchants have run Indian Ocean trade since ancient times, so Gujarati-speaking communities are found in East Africa, Britain and North America. After the division of Bombay State in 1960, Gujarati became the official language of the newly created state of Gujarat.

language.history: India's languages belong mainly to the Indo-European and Dravidian families; the languages of the north derive from Sanskrit and the Prakrits after it, while Tamil, Telugu and others in the south belong to the Dravidian family, and there are also languages of the Tibeto-Burman and Austroasiatic families. In the Middle Ages Persian was the court language of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire and deeply influenced the languages of northern India; British colonization made English the language of administration, law and higher education. After independence Hindi and English were made joint official languages of the Union, state boundaries were redrawn by language in 1956, and the schedule of the constitution now recognizes 22 languages, making a country where many languages coexist.

ranking.name: Biryani
ranking.description: Meat marinated in spices and yogurt and half-cooked long-grain rice are layered, saffron and fried onion added, and the pot is sealed and cooked over low heat; the aroma is rich.
ranking.history: The name is generally thought to come from Persian, and the dish matured in the court of the Mughal Empire, combining Persian rice dishes with Indian spices. After the decline of the Mughal Empire, different versions developed in different courts: the Nizam's court in Hyderabad is known for cooking raw meat and raw rice together, while the Awadhi version of Lucknow is milder; in 1856 the Nawab of Awadh, Wajid Ali Shah, was exiled by the British to Calcutta, and the local version there came to include potato. Today it is the most popular dish at Indian weddings, Eid and gatherings.

ranking.name: Butter chicken (murgh makhani)
ranking.description: Grilled chicken pieces are put into an orange-red thick sauce cooked from tomato, butter, cream and spices; the texture is rich and smooth, and it is eaten with naan.
ranking.history: Butter chicken was born after the Partition of 1947. Punjabi refugees from Peshawar (now in Pakistan), such as Kundan Lal Gujral, opened the Moti Mahal restaurant in Delhi, bringing the technique of cooking chicken in a clay oven (tandoor), and it is said that to keep unsold tandoori chicken from drying out, they soaked it in a tomato and butter sauce. Exactly who invented it is still disputed, even in court, between the restaurants concerned. It spread across India and the world with Punjabi migrants and became one of the best-known Indian dishes.

ranking.name: Masala dosa
ranking.description: A large thin crisp pancake fried on a griddle from a batter of fermented rice and black gram, wrapped around a spiced potato filling, and eaten with coconut chutney and lentil soup (sambar).
ranking.history: Dosa is an ancient food of South India, and early Tamil texts record similar rice pancakes. The potato is a crop introduced to India by the Portuguese in the 16th–17th centuries and later became the classic filling for dosa. In the 20th century, chefs from Udupi in Karnataka opened vegetarian restaurants in big cities such as Mumbai, spreading masala dosa across the country. It is the most common breakfast in South India and is especially classic in South Indian vegetarian restaurants.

ranking.name: Samosa
ranking.description: A triangular pastry shell made of flour is filled with spiced potato and green peas and deep-fried; the shell is crisp, and it is eaten with mint chutney or tamarind chutney.
ranking.history: The ancestor of the samosa is the Middle Eastern and Central Asian "sanbusak", which came to India in the 13th–14th centuries with Central Asian merchants and the court of the Delhi Sultanate; the poet Amir Khusrau and the traveler Ibn Battuta both recorded triangular pastries filled with minced meat in the court. After the potato arrived, the vegetarian version with a potato filling became common in India. Today it is India's most popular street snack and tea-time item, often served at festivals and at afternoon tea.

ranking.name: Chole bhature
ranking.description: Spicy chickpeas stewed with onion, tomato and many spices, served with puffy deep-fried leavened bread, often accompanied by pickles, onion and green chili.
ranking.history: Chole bhature is a representative food of Punjab. After the Partition of 1947, large numbers of Punjabi refugees flooded into Delhi, and they opened snack stalls and restaurants to make a living, making this dish quickly popular in Delhi and one of the capital's most representative breakfasts and lunches. It is hearty and cheap, reflecting the profound influence of the Partition migrants on the food culture of northern Indian cities.
